title: Whose is it?
goal: Express possession with two equally correct word orders — and know why Norwegians almost always choose the second one.
bekal: use *min/mi/mitt/mine* and the whole family of possessives
put the possessive **after** the noun — and keep its ending
say what belongs to someone with *-s* and with *til*
wave: Go back over **Unit 7** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Notice where *alltid*, *ofte* and *aldri* go in every sentence.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På vaskerommet
dialogs.intro: The laundry room in the basement. The third machine finished half an hour ago, and nobody seems to own what's inside it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nei, min er blå. Denne er grønn.
lines.id: No, mine is blue. This one's green.
lines.literal: no, mine is blue. this is green.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Kanskje det er Lars sin. Han glemmer alltid klærne sine.
lines.id: Maybe it's Lars's. He always forgets his clothes.
lines.literal: maybe it is Lars his. he forgets always the-clothes his-own.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Sannsynligvis. Hvor er håndkleet mitt, forresten?
lines.id: Probably. Where's my towel, by the way?
lines.literal: probably. where is the-towel mine, by-the-way?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ja! Takk. Og buksa di henger der.
lines.id: Yes! Thanks. And your trousers are hanging over there.
lines.literal: yes! thanks. and the-trousers yours hang there.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er ikke buksa mi. Den er altfor kort.
lines.id: Those aren't my trousers. They're far too short.
lines.literal: it is not the-trousers mine. it is all-too short.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da er den nok Lars sin også.
lines.literal: then is it probably Lars his also.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Lars eier hele vaskerommet, virker det som.
lines.id: Lars owns the whole laundry room, it seems.
lines.literal: Lars owns whole the-wash-room, seems it like.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nei, han bare glemmer. Vi legger alt i kurven hans.
lines.id: No, he just forgets. Let's put it all in his basket.
lines.literal: no, he just forgets. we put all in the-basket his.

notes: **This is the order to get used to: the possessive stands after the noun, and the noun keeps its ending.** *genseren din*, *håndkleet mitt*, *buksa mi*, *kurven hans*. Literally "the-sweater yours" — two markers at once.

**The opposite order is also correct**: *din genser*, *mitt håndkle*, *mi bukse*. But here the ending **drops** — not *din genseren*. This form is used when you want to stress who the owner is: *det er **min** genser, ikke din*.

**Which form should you use?** The one at the back. Norwegians use it in everyday conversation almost all the time, and the front form sounds emphatic or written. It feels backwards to an English speaker — and that's exactly why it needs practice. When in doubt, put it at the back.

**Buksa mi** — notice *mi*, not *min*. This is the special form for feminine nouns, and it's the natural partner of the *-a* ending. If you choose to write *buksen*, the partner becomes *buksen min*. Both are correct; don't mix them into *buksa min*.

**Lars sin** means "Lars's". This pattern — name + *sin/si/sitt/sine* — is the most common way in speech to say what belongs to someone. The formal version is *Lars' genser*, but hardly anyone says it that way.

**Klærne sine** uses *sine*, not *hans*, because the owner is the subject of the same sentence (*han glemmer*). The difference between *sin* and *hans* is the whole of the next unit — for now just notice that both exist.

grammars.title: The full set of possessives
body: The first three columns change with the gender of the noun; the rest don't change at all. Notice that **half of this table stands completely still** — a big saving.
after: Only four rows change: *min*, *din*, *vår* and *sin*. The other three (*hans*, *hennes*, *deres*) never move — learn one form and you're done.
If you choose to treat all *ei*-words as *en* (the shortcut from Unit 4), the second column disappears too and you're left with three forms per row.
*Deres* does two jobs at once — "your (plural)" and "their". The situation tells you which is meant, and in practice it's hardly ever confusing.

grammars.title: Two word orders, one meaning
body: Compare the two columns row by row. The difference to look for is in **the noun's ending**.
after: ⚠️ **The ending rule can't be broken.** In the left column the ending is required; in the right column it must go. *Min bilen* and *bil min* are both wrong.

English works like the right-hand column — "my car", owner in front — so that's the form your hand will reach for. Make yourself use the left-hand column: "the car of mine" is the closest English gets, and it's what Norwegians say all day long.

grammars.title: Someone's things: names, not pronouns
body: To say that something belongs to a particular person, Norwegian has three routes. The third is heard most, the first is written most.
after: ⚠️ **The -s ending never takes an apostrophe.** *Ingrids bil*, not *Ingrid's bil*. This English habit creeps in through shop signs and ads, and Norwegians themselves see it as a mistake.
If the name already ends in *-s*, *-x* or *-z*, just add an apostrophe: *Lars' genser*. But in conversation people will say *genseren til Lars* or *Lars sin genser*.

blocks.text: Practice possessives with things that are really around you. Say each row in both orders: *genseren min* and *min genser*.
Notice *ei skjorte* and *ei datamaskin* — the combinations *skj-* and *-sk-* before *i* both sound like **sh**. And *en sko* sounds like **skoo**, one more example of an *o* that turns into "oo".
Colors come up constantly when you're working out whose thing is whose, so they belong here. The second form is the one used with neuter nouns — the rule is in Unit 12.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Name ten things in your room with their owner and their color: *Det er genseren min. Den er blå.*
Then ask yourself about ten more things as if you were asking a roommate: *Er dette skjorta di?*
The hardest test: name five things belonging to someone else in all three patterns — *Ingrids bil*, *bilen til Ingrid*, *Ingrid sin bil*.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of *min*: *min*, *mi*, *mitt* or *mine*.
Rewrite with the possessive in front. Remember: the ending drops.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: min — mi — mitt — mine — min — mitt
